claim: Brain temperature has neurobiological and clinical importance.
source: Although brain temperature has neurobiological and clinical importance, it remains unclear which factors contribute to its daily dynamics and to what extent.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific understanding about brain temperature.

claim: Hourly brain temperature values co-varied strongly with time spent awake.
source: Using a statistical approach, we previously demonstrated that hourly brain temperature values co-varied strongly with time spent awake (Hoekstra et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The model estimated cortical temperature with remarkable precision and accounted for 91% of the variance.
source: Our model estimated cortical temperature with remarkable precision and accounted for 91% of the variance based on three factors: sleep–wake sequence, time-of-day ('circadian'), and a novel 'prior wake prevalence' factor, contributing with 74%, 9%, and 43%, respectively (including shared variance).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sleep–wake sequence contributes 74% to the variance in cortical temperature.
source: Our model estimated cortical temperature with remarkable precision and accounted for 91% of the variance based on three factors: sleep–wake sequence, time-of-day ('circadian'), and a novel 'prior wake prevalence' factor, contributing with 74%, 9%, and 43%, respectively (including shared variance).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model analysis.

claim: Time-of-day ('circadian') factor contributes 9% to the variance in cortical temperature.
source: Our model estimated cortical temperature with remarkable precision and accounted for 91% of the variance based on three factors: sleep–wake sequence, time-of-day ('circadian'), and a novel 'prior wake prevalence' factor, contributing with 74%, 9%, and 43%, respectively (including shared variance).

claim: The optimized parameters were applied to an independent cohort of mice and predicted cortical temperature with similar accuracy.
source: We applied these optimized parameters to an independent cohort of mice and predicted cortical temperature with similar accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by validation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The model confirms the profound influence of sleep–wake state on brain temperature.
source: This model confirms the profound influence of sleep–wake state on brain temperature, and can be harnessed to differentiate between thermoregulatory and sleep–wake-driven effects in experiments affecting both.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: Fluctuations within the physiological temperature range (33–37°C in rodents) have been shown to modify channel kinetics.
source: Specifically, fluctuations within the physiological temperature range (33–37°C in rodents) have been shown to modify channel kinetics (Rosen, 2001), reuptake of neurotransmitters by transporters (Xie et al., 2000), miniature postsynaptic currents (Simkus and Stricker, 2002), the neuronal firing rates of single neurons (Tryba and Ramirez, 2004; Guatteo et al., 2005), and neuronal synchronization (Csernai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Fluctuations within the physiological temperature range (33–37°C in rodents) have been shown to modify reuptake of neurotransmitters by transporters.
source: Specifically, fluctuations within the physiological temperature range (33–37°C in rodents) have been shown to modify channel kinetics (Rosen, 2001), reuptake of neurotransmitters by transporters (Xie et al., 2000), miniature postsynaptic currents (Simkus and Stricker, 2002), the neuronal firing rates of single neurons (Tryba and Ramirez, 2004; Guatteo et al., 2005), and neuronal synchronization (Csernai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Fluctuations within the physiological temperature range (33–37°C in rodents) have been shown to modify the neuronal firing rates of single neurons.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Neuronal activity is one of the main determinants of brain temperature.
source: Conversely, neuronal activity is one of the main determinants of brain temperature (Kiyatkin et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Brain activity both affects and is affected by fluctuations in temperature.
source: Thus, brain activity both affects and is affected by fluctuations in temperature.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bidirectional relationship described in the preceding sentences.

claim: Brain temperature increases in common pathological conditions such as stroke or head injury.
source: In clinical settings, brain temperature increases in common pathological conditions such as stroke or head injury (Mrozek et al., 2012), and temperature is deliberately lowered in interventions to protect the brain from hypoxic events (Faridar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior clinical research.

claim: Temperature is deliberately lowered in interventions to protect the brain from hypoxic events.
source: In clinical settings, brain temperature increases in common pathological conditions such as stroke or head injury (Mrozek et al., 2012), and temperature is deliberately lowered in interventions to protect the brain from hypoxic events (Faridar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior clinical research.

claim: Brain tissue is very sensitive to thermal damage.
source: Since heat plays a crucial role in neuronal functioning (Kiyatkin, 2010; Alonso and Marder, 2020) and brain tissue is very sensitive to thermal damage (Yarmolenko et al., 2011), it is crucial to understand which factors contribute to changes in brain temperature under normal circumstances.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Brain temperature is the net result of heat production and heat dissipation.
source: Generally, brain temperature is considered to be the net result of heat production, which is determined by brain metabolism, and heat dissipation, which is determined by brain blood flow and the brain-to-blood temperature gradient (Hayward and Baker, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Heat production is determined by brain metabolism.
source: Generally, brain temperature is considered to be the net result of heat production, which is determined by brain metabolism, and heat dissipation, which is determined by brain blood flow and the brain-to-blood temperature gradient (Hayward and Baker, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Heat dissipation is determined by brain blood flow and the brain-to-blood temperature gradient.
source: Generally, brain temperature is considered to be the net result of heat production, which is determined by brain metabolism, and heat dissipation, which is determined by brain blood flow and the brain-to-blood temperature gradient (Hayward and Baker, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Wakefulness and REM sleep are accompanied by increases in brain temperature.
source: The latter two (active) brain states are accompanied by increases in brain temperature, whereas NREM sleep evidences a decrease (Hayward and Baker, 1969; Obál et al., 1985; Franken et al., 1992a; Hoekstra et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: NREM sleep evidences a decrease in brain temperature.
source: The latter two (active) brain states are accompanied by increases in brain temperature, whereas NREM sleep evidences a decrease (Hayward and Baker, 1969; Obál et al., 1985; Franken et al., 1992a; Hoekstra et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Global blood flow to the brain decreases in absolute terms during NREM sleep.
source: Besides decreased heat production, increased heat dissipation further contributes to the decreases in brain temperature during NREM sleep: (i) although the global blood flow to the brain decreases in absolute terms, it increases when taking the considerable drop in oxygen consumption during NREM sleep into account (McAvoy et al., 2019), and (ii) since body temperature is actively down-regulated through peripheral vasodilation (and perspiration in humans) after sleep onset, the brain-to-blood temperature gradient increases (Szymusiak, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Blood flow to the brain increases relative to oxygen consumption during NREM sleep.
source: Besides decreased heat production, increased heat dissipation further contributes to the decreases in brain temperature during NREM sleep: (i) although the global blood flow to the brain decreases in absolute terms, it increases when taking the considerable drop in oxygen consumption during NREM sleep into account (McAvoy et al., 2019), and (ii) since body temperature is actively down-regulated through peripheral vasodilation (and perspiration in humans) after sleep onset, the brain-to-blood temperature gradient increases (Szymusiak, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Body temperature is actively down-regulated through peripheral vasodilation after sleep onset.
source: Besides decreased heat production, increased heat dissipation further contributes to the decreases in brain temperature during NREM sleep: (i) although the global blood flow to the brain decreases in absolute terms, it increases when taking the considerable drop in oxygen consumption during NREM sleep into account (McAvoy et al., 2019), and (ii) since body temperature is actively down-regulated through peripheral vasodilation (and perspiration in humans) after sleep onset, the brain-to-blood temperature gradient increases (Szymusiak, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The brain-to-blood temperature gradient increases after sleep onset.
source: Besides decreased heat production, increased heat dissipation further contributes to the decreases in brain temperature during NREM sleep: (i) although the global blood flow to the brain decreases in absolute terms, it increases when taking the considerable drop in oxygen consumption during NREM sleep into account (McAvoy et al., 2019), and (ii) since body temperature is actively down-regulated through peripheral vasodilation (and perspiration in humans) after sleep onset, the brain-to-blood temperature gradient increases (Szymusiak, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The sleep–wake distribution explains 84% of the variance in brain temperature in the rat.
source: By quantifying the relationship between sleep–wake state and brain temperature we reported that the sleep–wake distribution explains 84% of the variance in brain temperature in the rat (Franken et al., 1992b), a finding we recently replicated in the mouse (Hoekstra et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: The finding that sleep–wake distribution explains 84% of the variance in brain temperature was replicated in the mouse.
source: By quantifying the relationship between sleep–wake state and brain temperature we reported that the sleep–wake distribution explains 84% of the variance in brain temperature in the rat (Franken et al., 1992b), a finding we recently replicated in the mouse (Hoekstra et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: The 1992 analysis has been criticized for overestimating the impact of sleep–wake state by having averaged over hourly intervals.
source: However, the 1992 analysis has been criticized for overestimating the impact of sleep–wake state by having averaged over hourly intervals and ignoring other contributing factors such as locomotion (Heller et al., 2011), and the sequential nature of assessing the contribution of sleep–wake and circadian-related factors (Witting and Mirmiran, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to critical papers.

claim: The 1992 analysis has been criticized for ignoring other contributing factors such as locomotion.
source: However, the 1992 analysis has been criticized for overestimating the impact of sleep–wake state by having averaged over hourly intervals and ignoring other contributing factors such as locomotion (Heller et al., 2011), and the sequential nature of assessing the contribution of sleep–wake and circadian-related factors (Witting and Mirmiran, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a critical paper.

claim: Recent studies have found the contribution of locomotor activity to brain temperature to be negligible.
source: Although recent studies have found the contribution of locomotor activity to brain temperature to be negligible (Shirey et al., 2015; Hoekstra et al., 2019) and confirmed that circadian factors do not contribute significantly to brain temperature (Baker et al., 2005), the concerns underlying the use of hourly values and a fixed order of assessing the contributing factors have not been directly addressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Circadian factors do not contribute significantly to brain temperature.
source: Although recent studies have found the contribution of locomotor activity to brain temperature to be negligible (Shirey et al., 2015; Hoekstra et al., 2019) and confirmed that circadian factors do not contribute significantly to brain temperature (Baker et al., 2005), the concerns underlying the use of hourly values and a fixed order of assessing the contributing factors have not been directly addressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The new model explained 91% of the variance in brain temperature.
source: This new model explained 91% of the variance in brain temperature and reduced the model error to 0.26°C down from an observed dynamic range of 3.13°C.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model analysis.

claim: The new model reduced the model error to 0.26°C down from an observed dynamic range of 3.13°C.
source: This new model explained 91% of the variance in brain temperature and reduced the model error to 0.26°C down from an observed dynamic range of 3.13°C.

claim: The model revealed prior wake prevalence as a novel, longer-term factor altering the range of values within which brain temperature is regulated.
source: In addition to accurately capturing the short-term dynamics associated with sleep–wake transitions, the model revealed prior wake prevalence as a novel, longer-term factor altering the range of values within which brain temperature is regulated.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: The circadian factor explained 9.3% of the overall variance in brain temperature.
source: The circadian factor explained 9.3% of the overall variance in brain temperature, of which 7.6% was redundant with the contribution of the other two factors.

claim: Wakefulness and REM sleep can be considered to be the opposite of NREM sleep in brain temperature dynamics.
source: Wakefulness and REM sleep can be considered to be the opposite of NREM sleep in brain temperature dynamics.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed patterns in brain temperature.

claim: In the cortical activated states of wakefulness and REM sleep, brain temperature increases.
source: In the cortical activated states of wakefulness and REM sleep, brain temperature increases, whereas during NREM sleep when cortical input is reduced and neuronal activity becomes synchronized, temperature decreases (Obál et al., 1985; Franken et al., 1992a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During NREM sleep when cortical input is reduced and neuronal activity becomes synchronized, temperature decreases.
source: In the cortical activated states of wakefulness and REM sleep, brain temperature increases, whereas during NREM sleep when cortical input is reduced and neuronal activity becomes synchronized, temperature decreases (Obál et al., 1985; Franken et al., 1992a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Model 0 simulated the temperature recordings with an average correlation coefficient (r) of 0.91.
source: Based on this more refined model, referred to as Model 0, we simulated the temperature recordings based on the individual sleep–wake state sequence data (Figure 1), with an average correlation coefficient (r) of 0.91, and a median root mean square (RMS) error of 0.36°C across animals.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model analysis.

claim: Model 0 had a median root mean square (RMS) error of 0.36°C across animals.
source: Based on this more refined model, referred to as Model 0, we simulated the temperature recordings based on the individual sleep–wake state sequence data (Figure 1), with an average correlation coefficient (r) of 0.91, and a median root mean square (RMS) error of 0.36°C across animals.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model analysis.

claim: The time constant of wakefulness was higher than the one of NREM sleep in 9 out of 11 mice.
source: Generally, the time constant of wakefulness was higher than the one of NREM sleep (i.e., in 9 out of 11 mice; with median of 0.33 vs. 0.23 hr), indicating that the rate of increase of cortical temperature during wakefulness was slower than its decrease in NREM sleep.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model analysis.

claim: The difference between the upper and lower asymptotes varied by roughly 3°C.
source: The difference between the upper and lower asymptotes varied by roughly 3°C, with the upper asymptotes consistently near the temperature values observed during SD (Supplementary file 1).

claim: Incorporating a circadian modulation of both asymptotes somewhat improved the overall fit (RMS error = 0.32°C; residual RMS = 0.15°C).
source: Although incorporating a circadian modulation of both asymptotes as previously done in the rat (Franken et al., 1992b) somewhat improved the overall fit (RMS error = 0.32°C; residual RMS = 0.15°C), it did not abolish the apparent periodicity in the baseline residuals in mice and resulted in an even poorer fit during SD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model analysis.

claim: Incorporating a circadian modulation did not abolish the apparent periodicity in the baseline residuals in mice.
source: Although incorporating a circadian modulation of both asymptotes as previously done in the rat (Franken et al., 1992b) somewhat improved the overall fit (RMS error = 0.32°C; residual RMS = 0.15°C), it did not abolish the apparent periodicity in the baseline residuals in mice and resulted in an even poorer fit during SD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the model analysis.

claim: Incorporating a circadian modulation resulted in an even poorer fit during SD.

evidence: This is an observation from the model analysis supported by a figure.

claim: Modulation of the asymptotes according to prior wake prevalence considerably improved the fit (r = 0.95; RMS error = 0.28°C).
source: Modulation of the asymptotes according to prior wake prevalence considerably improved the fit (r = 0.95; RMS error = 0.28°C; Figure 2) and removed most of the excessive overestimations during light periods, as well as the underestimation of temperature during the dark periods (see arrows in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model analysis.

claim: The optimal window size for prior wake prevalence was 4.0 hr.
source: We found that the optimal window size was 4.0 hr, with a shift of 1.5 hr prior to the time point under consideration, and a scaling factor of 1.2°C.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model optimization.

claim: The optimal shift for prior wake prevalence was 1.5 hr prior to the time point under consideration.

claim: All parameter values obtained with Model 0 changed significantly when optimized in Model 1 (p≤0.002; F(2,10) ≥ 9.98).
source: We optimized all the parameters simultaneously in this new model (i.e., Model 1) and found that all of the values obtained with Model 0 changed significantly (p≤0.002; F(2,10) ≥ 9.98, one-way repeated measures analysis of variance [rANOVA]): the lower asymptote increased, leading to a substantial reduction in the inter-asymptote temperature range from 3.1°C to 2.0°C, which might have contributed to the substantial shortening of the time constants (0.18 and 0.13 hr for wake/REM sleep and NREM sleep, respectively), as they need to be faster to compensate for the reduced distance from the asymptote so that a similar increase/decrease temperature rate can be achieved.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the model analysis.

claim: The lower asymptote increased in Model 1.
source: We optimized all the parameters simultaneously in this new model (i.e., Model 1) and found that all of the values obtained with Model 0 changed significantly (p≤0.002; F(2,10) ≥ 9.98, one-way repeated measures analysis of variance [rANOVA]): the lower asymptote increased, leading to a substantial reduction in the inter-asymptote temperature range from 3.1°C to 2.0°C, which might have contributed to the substantial shortening of the time constants (0.18 and 0.13 hr for wake/REM sleep and NREM sleep, respectively), as they need to be faster to compensate for the reduced distance from the asymptote so that a similar increase/decrease temperature rate can be achieved.

evidence: This is a quantitative result from the prediction analysis on an independent cohort.

claim: Repeating the process for the test group with the medians of Model 1 yielded correlation coefficients in the 0.91–0.93 range.
source: Repeating this process for the test group with the medians of the more basic models 0 and 1, yielded correlation coefficients in the 0.86–0.89 and 0.91–0.93 ranges, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the prediction analysis on an independent cohort.

claim: At any given time of the experiment, the range of observed temperature fluctuations did not surpass 2°C.
source: In mice kept under our experimental conditions, specifically a 25°C ambient temperature, a 12:12 hr light–dark cycle, housed singly, and food ad libitum, we observed a dynamic brain temperature range of a little over 3°C. However, at any given time of the experiment, the range of observed temperature fluctuations did not surpass 2°C.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The 2°C range represents a homeostatically defended range within which the brain temperature can vary according to the animal's behavior without eliciting a thermoregulatory response.
source: This range, delimited by the upper and lower asymptotes in the model, represents a homeostatically defended range within which the brain temperature can vary according to the animal's behavior without eliciting a thermoregulatory response (Parmeggiani et al., 1975; Satinoff, 1983).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous work in rats maintained under different photoperiods and under constant dark conditions arrived at very similar amplitudes for the time-of-day modulation of cortical temperature (0.13–0.21°C).
source: Nevertheless, using a different analytical approach, our previous work in rats maintained under different photoperiods and under constant dark conditions arrived at very similar amplitudes for the time-of-day modulation of cortical temperature (0.13–0.21°C; Franken et al., 1992b; Franken et al., 1995), supporting the interpretation that the time-of-day factor does not depend on the lighting condition and is likely to represent a modulation of circadian origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research by the authors.

claim: The time-of-day factor does not depend on the lighting condition and is likely to represent a modulation of circadian origin.
source: Nevertheless, using a different analytical approach, our previous work in rats maintained under different photoperiods and under constant dark conditions arrived at very similar amplitudes for the time-of-day modulation of cortical temperature (0.13–0.21°C; Franken et al., 1992b; Franken et al., 1995), supporting the interpretation that the time-of-day factor does not depend on the lighting condition and is likely to represent a modulation of circadian origin.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by prior research findings.

claim: Up-regulation of brain temperature during sustained wakefulness has been reported previously under conditions of SD spanning several weeks.
source: Up-regulation of brain temperature during sustained wakefulness has been reported previously but was observed under conditions of SD spanning several weeks (Obermeyer et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The onset of NREM sleep is associated with an active down-regulation of brain temperature involving peripheral vasodilation concomitant with decreased neural activity.
source: The onset of NREM sleep is associated with an active down-regulation of brain temperature involving peripheral vasodilation concomitant with decreased neural activity (Glotzbach and Heller, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The time constants were in the range of minutes for both the increases during wakefulness (and REM sleep) and the decreases in cortical temperature during NREM sleep.
source: The simulation identified time constants in the range of minutes for both the increases during wakefulness (and REM sleep) and the decreases in cortical temperature during NREM sleep.
evidence: This is a result from the model analysis.

claim: The simulation found longer time constants for the increase than for the decrease (13 and 7 min, respectively).
source: It also found longer time constants for the increase than for the decrease (13 and 7 min, respectively), pointing to a slower buildup of heat relative to its dissipation during NREM sleep.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model analysis.

claim: The difference in time constants points to a slower buildup of heat relative to its dissipation during NREM sleep.
source: It also found longer time constants for the increase than for the decrease (13 and 7 min, respectively), pointing to a slower buildup of heat relative to its dissipation during NREM sleep.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the time constant results.

claim: The difference in time constants is consistent with the concept that the blood that perfuses the brain acts as a heat sink.
source: This difference is consistent with the concept that the blood that perfuses the brain acts as a heat sink, and that increases in temperature underestimate the rate of heat production since cooling occurs simultaneously (Hayward and Baker, 1969).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Increases in temperature underestimate the rate of heat production since cooling occurs simultaneously.
source: This difference is consistent with the concept that the blood that perfuses the brain acts as a heat sink, and that increases in temperature underestimate the rate of heat production since cooling occurs simultaneously (Hayward and Baker, 1969).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Model 0 explained 83% of the variance.
source: As suggested previously (Franken et al., 1992b), the circadian factor carried surprisingly little information about brain temperature. Of the 9% of the variance that could be attributed to circadian modulation, most was redundant with that of the other two factors and only <2% was uniquely circadian. In the model, both the circadian and prior wake-prevalence factors modulated the asymptotes. Consistent with the fivefold larger portion of variance explained by the latter, the maximum possible modulation of the asymptote was also fivefold larger.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model analysis.

claim: The circadian factor carried surprisingly little information about brain temperature.
source: As suggested previously (Franken et al., 1992b), the circadian factor carried surprisingly little information about brain temperature.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The maximum possible modulation of the asymptote by prior wake prevalence was fivefold larger than that by circadian modulation.
source: In the model, both the circadian and prior wake-prevalence factors modulated the asymptotes. Consistent with the fivefold larger portion of variance explained by the latter, the maximum possible modulation of the asymptote was also fivefold larger.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model analysis.

claim: In the previous model, only the time constants were optimized but the estimates for the asymptotes were taken directly from the data.
source: Compared to our earlier effort to simulate brain temperature in the rat (Franken et al., 1992b), we made a number of key modifications that enhanced the accuracy of the simulation. In the previous model, only the time constants were optimized but the estimates for the asymptotes were taken directly from the data.
evidence: This describes a methodological difference from prior work.

claim: In the previous model, the same time constants were used to simulate the increases and decreases in temperature accompanying sleep–wake state transitions.
source: Moreover, the same time constants were used to simulate the increases and decreases in temperature accompanying sleep–wake state transitions.
evidence: This describes a methodological difference from prior work.

claim: The amplitude of the time-of-day modulation was surprisingly similar in the two studies and species.
source: The first such factor is the time-of-day ('circadian') modulation, whose amplitude was surprisingly similar in the two studies and species.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study and prior work.

claim: In the rat study, a down-regulation of the asymptote was needed to accurately fit the initial 12 hr of recovery.
source: Moreover, in the rat study, a down-regulation of the asymptote was needed to accurately fit the initial 12 hr of recovery because the actual temperature levels were lower than those predicted based on the sleep–wake distribution.
evidence: This describes a finding from prior work.

claim: This down-regulation after SD was not observed in the current study even when the prior wake-prevalence factor was not incorporated.
source: This down-regulation after SD was not observed in the current study even when the prior wake-prevalence factor was not incorporated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study.

claim: The time constants in the rat (0.47 hr) were considerably slower than in the mouse.
source: The final difference between the two studies is the considerably slower time constants in the rat (0.47 hr) compared to the mouse, which may be attributed to a species difference.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study and prior work.

claim: The sequential evaluation of the contribution of different factors may lead to an overestimation of those assessed first because shared (or redundant) variance will be added to the first but not the second.
source: As previously noted by others (e.g., Witting and Mirmiran, 1997), the sequential evaluation of the contribution of different factors may lead to an overestimation of those assessed first because shared (or redundant) variance will be added to the first but not the second.
evidence: This is a methodological concern raised by prior research.

claim: Performance assessed at a 4 s resolution yielded high correlations similar to the hourly values.
source: We found no support for this criticism: performance assessed at a 4 s resolution yielded high correlations similar to the hourly values (Franken et al., 1992b).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study that addresses prior criticism.

claim: Brain temperature dynamics during sleep–wake state transitions seem qualitatively similar across a wide range of ambient temperatures.
source: Although brain temperature dynamics during sleep–wake state transitions seem qualitatively similar across a wide range of ambient temperatures (Alföldi et al., 1990), it is nevertheless likely that the model parameters, and in particular the time constants, would need to be optimized for each ambient temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: It is likely that the model parameters, and in particular the time constants, would need to be optimized for each ambient temperature.
source: Although brain temperature dynamics during sleep–wake state transitions seem qualitatively similar across a wide range of ambient temperatures (Alföldi et al., 1990), it is nevertheless likely that the model parameters, and in particular the time constants, would need to be optimized for each ambient temperature.
evidence: This is a speculation about model generalization.

claim: Increases in brain temperature accompanying intense activity such as wheel running cannot be captured by the current version of the model.
source: Moreover, increases in brain temperature accompanying intense activity such as wheel running (Fuller et al., 1998; Kunstetter et al., 2014), or activating stimuli such as a tail pinch or cage change (Kiyatkin et al., 2002), cannot be captured by the current version of our model because we considered wakefulness to be a uniform brain state.
evidence: This is a limitation of the current model acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The model could be easily expanded to accommodate additional factors, once experimental data are available.
source: Although these refinements of the simulation are currently lacking, the model could be easily expanded to accommodate these factors, once experimental data are available.
evidence: This is a speculation about future model development.

claim: Rhythms in temperature are generally considered a direct output of the circadian time-keeping system.
source: Rhythms in temperature are generally considered a direct output of the circadian time-keeping system (Refinetti and Menaker, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and represents established knowledge.

claim: The circadian contribution to brain temperature in the mouse is small.
source: Our model showed, however, that the circadian contribution to brain temperature in the mouse is small and that the observed circadian rhythmicity in brain temperature under undisturbed conditions is driven primarily by the circadian sleep–wake distribution.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The observed circadian rhythmicity in brain temperature under undisturbed conditions is driven primarily by the circadian sleep–wake distribution.
source: Our model showed, however, that the circadian contribution to brain temperature in the mouse is small and that the observed circadian rhythmicity in brain temperature under undisturbed conditions is driven primarily by the circadian sleep–wake distribution.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: In rodents in general, body and brain temperatures change in parallel.
source: In rodents in general, body and brain temperatures change in parallel (Blessing, 2018), suggesting that their gross dynamics are governed by similar rules and that the daily dynamics (e.g., hourly mean values) of body temperature can be predicted using assumptions similar to those in our model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The gross dynamics of body and brain temperature are governed by similar rules.
source: In rodents in general, body and brain temperatures change in parallel (Blessing, 2018), suggesting that their gross dynamics are governed by similar rules and that the daily dynamics (e.g., hourly mean values) of body temperature can be predicted using assumptions similar to those in our model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the parallel changes in body and brain temperature.

claim: At the finer time scale, the temperatures of the brain and body behave differently.
source: However, at the finer time scale at which we optimized our model, the few available studies suggest that the temperatures of the brain and body behave differently (Ootsuka et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Body temperature does not increase during REM sleep.
source: One noticeable example of this is that body temperature does not increase during REM sleep (Alföldi et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: During extreme sleep disturbance or thermal manipulations, brain and body temperatures can deviate considerably.
source: Moreover, during extreme sleep disturbance (Obermeyer et al., 1991; Baud et al., 2013) or thermal manipulations (Donhoffer et al., 1959; Kiley et al., 1984), brain and body temperatures can deviate considerably, suggesting that their underlying regulatory mechanisms differ.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The underlying regulatory mechanisms of brain and body temperature differ.
source: Moreover, during extreme sleep disturbance (Obermeyer et al., 1991; Baud et al., 2013) or thermal manipulations (Donhoffer et al., 1959; Kiley et al., 1984), brain and body temperatures can deviate considerably, suggesting that their underlying regulatory mechanisms differ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed deviations between brain and body temperature.

claim: Neuroactive drugs affect brain temperature.
source: For instance, neuroactive drugs do not only affect brain temperature (Kiyatkin, 2018) but often also impact the sleep–wake state.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Neuroactive drugs often impact the sleep–wake state.
source: For instance, neuroactive drugs do not only affect brain temperature (Kiyatkin, 2018) but often also impact the sleep–wake state.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge.

claim: Brain temperature affects many properties of neuronal functioning.
source: Second, brain temperature affects many properties of neuronal functioning (Kiyatkin, 2010) and therefore may influence cognitive performance (Walter and Carraretto, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Brain temperature may influence cognitive performance.
source: Second, brain temperature affects many properties of neuronal functioning (Kiyatkin, 2010) and therefore may influence cognitive performance (Walter and Carraretto, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: One study reported similar temperature dynamics in humans to those in the mouse.
source: Although such data in humans are sparse, one study reported similar temperature dynamics to those in the mouse (Landolt et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Studies in rodents have shown that locomotor activity only has a minimal association with brain temperature.
source: Since studies in rodents have shown that both locomotor activity (Shirey et al., 2015; Hoekstra et al., 2019) and NREM sleep depth (Franken et al., 1991; Tobler et al., 1994) only have a minimal association with brain temperature, brain temperature in humans might be driven by the sleep–wake distribution, consistent with the assumptions of our simulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Studies in rodents have shown that NREM sleep depth only has a minimal association with brain temperature.
source: Since studies in rodents have shown that both locomotor activity (Shirey et al., 2015; Hoekstra et al., 2019) and NREM sleep depth (Franken et al., 1991; Tobler et al., 1994) only have a minimal association with brain temperature, brain temperature in humans might be driven by the sleep–wake distribution, consistent with the assumptions of our simulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Brain temperature in humans might be driven by the sleep–wake distribution.
source: Since studies in rodents have shown that both locomotor activity (Shirey et al., 2015; Hoekstra et al., 2019) and NREM sleep depth (Franken et al., 1991; Tobler et al., 1994) only have a minimal association with brain temperature, brain temperature in humans might be driven by the sleep–wake distribution, consistent with the assumptions of our simulation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on findings in rodents.

claim: Data from 11 male C57BL6/J mice were included in the study.
source: Data from 11 male C57BL6/J mice (seven wild types [WT]) and four lacking the gene encoding cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (Cirbp KO mice), 10–15 weeks of age were included.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects.

claim: Sleep–wake distribution and brain temperature were unaltered in KO mice.
source: Sleep–wake distribution and brain temperature were unaltered in KO mice (Hoekstra et al., 2019) and likewise the results reported here did not differ statistically between the two genotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and current findings.

claim: All mice were housed individually under a 12:12 hr light–dark cycle.
source: All mice were housed individually under a 12:12 hr light–dark cycle with ZT0 and ZT12, corresponding to light onset and dark onset, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Ambient temperature was maintained at 25°C.
source: Ambient temperature was maintained at 25°C and food and water were provided ad libitum.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions.

claim: Brain temperature was measured by a thermistor placed on top of the right visual cortex.
source: Brain temperature was measured by a thermistor placed on top of the right visual cortex corresponding to the midpoint of the frontal-parietal EEG electrode pair on the left hemisphere, and was sampled at 10 Hz and the median value for each 4 s epoch represented that epoch.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Recordings lasted 96 hr and started at light onset.
source: Recordings lasted 96 hr, started at light onset, and included two 24 hr days serving as baseline (termed baseline 1 and baseline 2), 6 hr of SD starting at light onset on day 3, followed by an 18-hr (recovery 1) and a 24-hr (recovery 2) recovery period.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: SD was achieved by gentle handling.
source: SD was achieved by gentle handling (Mang and Franken, 2012).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

source: All experiments were approved by the Ethics Committee of the State of Vaud Veterinary Office Switzerland under license VD2743 and VD3201.
